figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Graph RAG pipeline using an LLM-derived graph index of source document text. This graph index spans nodes (e.g., entities), edges (e.g., relationships), and covariates (e.g., claims) that have been detected, extracted, and summarized by LLM prompts tailored to the domain of the dataset. Community detection (e.g., Leiden, Traag et al.,, 2019) is used to partition the graph index into groups of elements (nodes, edges, covariates) that the LLM can summarize in parallel at both indexing time and query time. The “global answer” to a given query is produced using a final round of query-focused summarization over all community summaries reporting relevance to that query.
figures.headline: The Graph RAG pipeline builds an LLM-derived graph index, partitions it into communities, and summarizes them for answering queries.

Circles represent entity nodes with size proportional to their degree. Node layout was performed via OpenORD (Martin et al.,, 2011) and Force Atlas 2 (Jacomy et al.,, 2014). Node colors represent entity communities, shown at two levels of hierarchical clustering: (a) Level 0, corresponding to the hierarchical partition with maximum modularity, and (b) Level 1, which reveals internal structure within these root-level communities.

abstract: The use of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to retrieve relevant information from an external knowledge source enables large language models (LLMs) to answer questions over private and/or previously unseen document collections. However, RAG fails on global questions directed at an entire text corpus, such as “What are the main themes in the dataset?”, since this is inherently a query-focused summarization (QFS) task, rather than an explicit retrieval task. Prior QFS methods, meanwhile, do not scale to the quantities of text indexed by typical RAG systems. To combine the strengths of these contrasting methods, we propose GraphRAG, a graph-based approach to question answering over private text corpora that scales with both the generality of user questions and the quantity of source text. Our approach uses an LLM to build a graph index in two stages: first, to derive an entity knowledge graph from the source documents, then to pregenerate community summaries for all groups of closely related entities. Given a question, each community summary is used to generate a partial response, before all partial responses are again summarized in a final response to the user. For a class of global sensemaking questions over datasets in the 1 million token range, we show that GraphRAG leads to substantial improvements over a conventional RAG baseline for both the comprehensiveness and diversity of generated answers.

sections.body: The paper introduces GraphRAG, which uses an LLM to build a knowledge graph from source documents, partitions the graph into hierarchical communities of related entities, and generates community summaries bottom-up. Queries are answered by map-reduce processing of these summaries. The authors state that vector RAG is unable to support sensemaking over an entire corpus. They compare GraphRAG with vector RAG using an LLM-as-a-judge method on generated questions, and report that GraphRAG strongly outperforms vector RAG when using GPT-4 as the LLM. They describe the GraphRAG method and its global sensemaking ability as the main contribution.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: RAG cannot answer corpus-wide sensemaking questions, so GraphRAG builds an entity graph with community summaries and outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4.

sections.body: This section places GraphRAG among prior work. It relates GraphRAG to hierarchical summarization and self-memory, to LLM-based knowledge graph extraction, and to graph-based retrieval. It states that benchmarks such as HotPotQA, MultiHop-RAG and MT-Bench are oriented toward vector RAG performance, meaning explicit fact retrieval. The authors describe an adaptive benchmarking method in which LLM-generated personas and tasks produce corpus-specific sensemaking questions. The evaluation criteria rely on pairwise LLM judgments, with claim-based statistics used to validate results.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Prior work covers graph-based retrieval, hierarchical summaries and benchmarks oriented toward explicit fact retrieval rather than global questions.

sections.body: Documents are split into text chunks, and the LLM extracts entities, relationships and claims from each chunk. Duplicate instances become graph nodes and edges, and duplicate relationships become edge weights. Leiden community detection is applied recursively to form a hierarchy of communities. The LLM writes a summary for each community, and high-level summaries incorporate lower-level ones. At query time, shuffled community summaries produce scored partial answers, and answers scored 0 are filtered out. The remaining answers are combined into a global answer. Exact string matching is used for entity matching in this analysis.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects Leiden communities, summarizes them, and answers queries by map-reduce over summaries.

sections.body: The two datasets are Behind the Tech podcast transcripts, about 1 million tokens, and a news articles benchmark, about 1.7 million tokens. Six conditions are compared: GraphRAG community levels C0 to C3, a map-reduce summary of source texts (TS), and vector RAG semantic search (SS). All conditions use an 8k token context window. Questions are generated from personas and their tasks for each dataset. Experiment 2 validates comprehensiveness and diversity with claims extracted by Claimify, which yielded 47,075 unique claims with an average of 31 claims per answer.
sections.heading: Analysis
sections.headline: Experiments compare six conditions on two corpora of about one million tokens, using generated global sensemaking questions.

sections.body: Global approaches significantly outperformed vector RAG on comprehensiveness and diversity across both datasets (p<.001 for most comparisons). Comprehensiveness win rates were 72-83% for podcast transcripts and 72-80% for news articles. Diversity win rates were 75-82% and 62-71%. Empowerment results were mixed. Root-level summaries (C0) required over 97% fewer tokens than source text summarization, while C3 required 26-33% fewer tokens. In the claim-based check, the average claim count of SS was lower than all global conditions, and the LLM label matched the claim-based label in 78% of non-tied comprehensiveness comparisons.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Global GraphRAG conditions beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness at 72-83% win rates on podcast transcripts.

sections.body: The authors state that their evaluation focuses on sensemaking questions for two corpora, each containing approximately 1 million tokens, so performance on other domains remains unknown. They say a comparison of fabrication rates, for example with SelfCheckGPT, would strengthen the analysis. Future work includes hybrid schemes that combine embedding-based matching with just-in-time community report generation, and drill-down mechanisms. The broader impacts section notes risks if generated answers misrepresent source data, and states that GraphRAG shows promise for mitigating downstream risks for global questions compared with vector RAG.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Evaluation covers only two corpora and lacks a fabrication-rate comparison, which the authors name as limitations.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that GraphRAG combines knowledge graph generation and query-focused summarization to support sensemaking over entire text corpora. It reports substantial improvements over a vector RAG baseline for comprehensiveness and diversity, and favorable comparisons with map-reduce source text summarization. For many global queries over the same dataset, the authors state that root-level community summaries provide an index that is superior to vector RAG and achieves competitive performance with other global methods at a fraction of the token cost.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Root-level community summaries give a data index that beats vector RAG and competes with other global methods at lower token cost.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the entity and claim extraction prompts for GPT-4 and describes self-reflection, in which the LLM is asked to glean missed entities. Appendix B gives an example of community detection. Appendix C tests context windows of 8k, 16k, 32k and 64k tokens. The 8k window had an average comprehensiveness win rate of 58.1%, and was therefore used for the final evaluation. Appendix D shows an example question with two answers and the LLM decisions. Appendix E gives the system prompts for element instance generation and community summary generation.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists extraction prompts, self-reflection gleaning, community detection, context window tests, an example comparison, and system prompts.
